As a starting point, the answer is no: eating the eggs reinforces the idea that the hen exists to serve, sets an example for those watching, and, if the hen was bought, the purchase funds hatcheries that cull the males. There is a controversial answer that some animal advocates give: yes, but only if all the hen's conditions are respected. A rescued hen living in a backyard has no connection to the egg industry, which culls male chicks and confines laying hens. Today's hens lay many more eggs than wild hens used to, because people bred them for that. Laying so many eggs tires out their bodies. That's why some people who care for rescued hens give the eggs back to them to eat, so they can get their strength back.

It's a rare case, and it has nothing to do with store-bought eggs, which come from an industry that culls male chicks and confines hens. Even in your backyard, there are good reasons not to eat them: modern hens lay close to 300 eggs a year, far more than their wild ancestors, and that depletes the calcium in their bodies. Many sanctuaries give the eggs back to the hens to help them recover, and you can do the same for yours. So, as a starting point, the answer is no: eating the eggs reinforces the idea that the hen exists to serve and encourages others. Some animal advocates accept, controversially, eating leftover eggs, but only with a rescued hen, no breeding, her health first and nothing sold. And even if that exception were accepted, it wouldn't justify the rule: it doesn't make buying eggs acceptable.

text.bold: 2. Even if accepted, the exception wouldn't justify the rule.

paragraph.text: Suppose that eating the eggs of a rescued hen, with every condition respected, isn't wrong. That doesn't make buying eggs acceptable. What would make the case acceptable (no connection to the industry and no harm to the hen) is exactly what store-bought eggs lack. A well-defined exception confirms the criterion; it doesn't overturn it.

text.bold: 3. The industry is what's in question.

paragraph.text: Store-bought eggs involve culling billions of male chicks a year and slaughtering laying hens when production drops (B5).
Modern laying hens lay close to 300 eggs a year, while their wild ancestors laid a few dozen. This demands a lot of calcium and energy, and is linked to health problems.
Many sanctuaries offer the eggs back to the hens, who eat them and recover nutrients. The "wasted" egg is useful to the one who produced it.

text.bold: 6. Eating the egg reinforces the idea that the hen is for this.

paragraph.text: Even without direct harm, treating the hen as a source of food keeps the category of "production animal" alive (C10).
Someone who sees an animal advocate eating their own hen's eggs tends to conclude that eating eggs is fine, and will almost always buy them at the store rather than rescue a hen.

text.bold: 8. A bought hen is not a harmless case.

paragraph.text: Hens sold as pets usually come from the same hatcheries that sex the chicks and cull the males. Buying a hen to have eggs at home funds that system; rescuing a hen from the industry does not.

text.bold: The controversial answer exists, but it is narrow.

paragraph.text: Some animal advocates accept eating the eggs if all these conditions are met: the hen was rescued, not bought; there is no rooster and no breeding; she gets veterinary care, including for the problems common in laying hens; her diet replaces calcium, and she can eat her own eggs when she needs to; only leftover eggs are used; nothing is sold or given away in a way that encourages breeding; and it is not presented to others as a model. Even then, points 6 and 7 still apply, and many advocates prefer not to eat them.

text.bold: The philosophical basis of the controversial answer.

paragraph.text: The political philosopher Alasdair Cochrane argues that most animals have no intrinsic interest in liberty: liberty matters to them for the well-being it brings, not in itself, because they don't frame or revise their own conception of a good life. For him, sentient animals have a right not to suffer and not to be killed, but using animals isn't wrong in itself. On this view, the question about the rescued hen isn't "use or don't use", but "does this harm her?", which leads back to the conditions above and to her health. Cochrane's view is contested: authors such as Robert Garner and Eva Meijer argue that animals do have an interest in liberty, and the abolitionist approach holds that treating animals as a resource is wrong even without apparent harm. And even on Cochrane's theory, store-bought eggs remain condemned, because the industry kills the male chicks and the laying hens.

The rescued hen's case is genuinely different from the industry. People who rescue hens do something good, and there's no cruelty comparable to that of factory farms in a well-kept backyard. It's also true that veganism shouldn't get lost in formalism.

But the case says nothing about store-bought eggs. And on closer inspection, even the backyard egg has a cost to the hen, and it can be given back to her. That is why the starting answer is no, and the controversial yes only holds with all of the hen's conditions put first.
